notes.markdown:
# 2.1 Antiderivatives

Reverse differentiation, constants of integration, and families of curves.

## Core idea

An antiderivative of a function is another function whose derivative gives the original function.

Indefinite integration describes a family of antiderivatives. The constant of integration accounts for functions that have the same derivative but differ by a vertical translation.

## Rules to remember

Apply the power rule term by term when the exponent is not negative one.

Always include the constant of integration for an indefinite integral.

Differentiate the result to check an antiderivative quickly.

notes.title: Partial fractions

sections.title: Before decomposing
body: First check that the rational expression is proper. If the numerator degree is at least the denominator degree, perform polynomial division.

notes.title: Wave characteristics
notes.summary: Describing periodic disturbances with wavelength, frequency, amplitude, and speed.

sections.title: The four quantities
body: A wave transfers energy through a medium without transferring the medium itself. Wavelength is the distance between successive points in phase, and frequency is the number of complete oscillations passing a point each second.
Wave speed follows from the two: $v = f\lambda$. In a uniform medium the speed is fixed by the medium, so raising the frequency shortens the wavelength.

sections.title: Transverse and longitudinal
body: In a transverse wave the oscillation is perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer; in a longitudinal wave it is parallel, producing compressions and rarefactions.
Sound in air is longitudinal. Light and all electromagnetic radiation is transverse, which is why light can be polarised and sound cannot.
sections.callout: Clarified after a class question: amplitude sets the energy carried, not the speed. A louder sound and a quieter one travel at the same speed.

sections.title: Reading the two graphs
body: A displacement-distance graph read at one instant shows wavelength. A displacement-time graph read at one point shows period. Check the axis label before quoting either value.

notes.markdown:
# 4.1 Wave characteristics

Describing periodic disturbances with wavelength, frequency, amplitude, and speed.

## The four quantities

A wave transfers energy through a medium without transferring the medium itself. Wavelength is the distance between successive points in phase, and frequency is the number of complete oscillations passing a point each second.

Wave speed follows from the two: $v = f\lambda$. In a uniform medium the speed is fixed by the medium, so raising the frequency shortens the wavelength.

## Transverse and longitudinal

In a transverse wave the oscillation is perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer; in a longitudinal wave it is parallel, producing compressions and rarefactions.

Sound in air is longitudinal. Light and all electromagnetic radiation is transverse, which is why light can be polarised and sound cannot.

> Clarified after a class question: amplitude sets the energy carried, not the speed. A louder sound and a quieter one travel at the same speed.

## Reading the two graphs

A displacement-distance graph read at one instant shows wavelength. A displacement-time graph read at one point shows period. Check the axis label before quoting either value.

notes.title: Wave behaviour
notes.summary: Reflection, refraction, diffraction, and superposition at boundaries and gaps.

sections.title: At a boundary
body: Reflection returns the wave into its original medium with the angle of incidence equal to the angle of reflection.
Refraction changes the direction because the speed changes. Frequency is set by the source and does not change, so the wavelength changes instead.

sections.title: Superposition
body: Where two waves meet, displacements add. Equal and opposite displacements cancel, giving destructive interference; displacements in phase reinforce.
A path difference of a whole number of wavelengths gives constructive interference; an odd number of half wavelengths gives destructive.

notes.markdown:
# 4.2 Wave behaviour

Reflection, refraction, diffraction, and superposition at boundaries and gaps.

## At a boundary

Reflection returns the wave into its original medium with the angle of incidence equal to the angle of reflection.

Refraction changes the direction because the speed changes. Frequency is set by the source and does not change, so the wavelength changes instead.

## Superposition

Where two waves meet, displacements add. Equal and opposite displacements cancel, giving destructive interference; displacements in phase reinforce.

A path difference of a whole number of wavelengths gives constructive interference; an odd number of half wavelengths gives destructive.

notes.title: The mole concept
notes.summary: Counting particles by mass, and the arithmetic that connects the two.

sections.title: What a mole counts
body: One mole is $6.02\times10^{23}$ particles. The molar mass in grams per mole is numerically equal to the relative formula mass, which is what makes the laboratory balance a particle counter.
Number of moles is mass divided by molar mass. Keep the formula and the units together; most lost marks here come from quoting a mass where a number of moles was asked for.

sections.title: Empirical and molecular formulae
body: An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms. Convert each mass or percentage to moles, divide through by the smallest, then scale to whole numbers.
The molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula, found by comparing the relative molecular mass to the empirical formula mass.
sections.callout: Added after marking: divide by the smallest number of moles, not by the smallest mass. Doing it by mass is the single most common error on this topic.

sections.title: Limiting reactant
body: Convert every reactant to moles, divide by its coefficient in the balanced equation, and the smallest result identifies the limiting reactant. Every yield is calculated from that reactant alone.

notes.markdown:
# 1.1 The mole concept

Counting particles by mass, and the arithmetic that connects the two.

## What a mole counts

One mole is $6.02\times10^{23}$ particles. The molar mass in grams per mole is numerically equal to the relative formula mass, which is what makes the laboratory balance a particle counter.

Number of moles is mass divided by molar mass. Keep the formula and the units together; most lost marks here come from quoting a mass where a number of moles was asked for.

## Empirical and molecular formulae

An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms. Convert each mass or percentage to moles, divide through by the smallest, then scale to whole numbers.

The molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula, found by comparing the relative molecular mass to the empirical formula mass.

> Added after marking: divide by the smallest number of moles, not by the smallest mass. Doing it by mass is the single most common error on this topic.

## Limiting reactant

Convert every reactant to moles, divide by its coefficient in the balanced equation, and the smallest result identifies the limiting reactant. Every yield is calculated from that reactant alone.

steps: Let the sides be x and y, so 2x + 2y = 40 and y = 20 − x.
Area A(x) = x(20 − x) = 20x − x².

A″(x) = −2 < 0, so it is a maximum. Sides 10 cm, area 100 cm².
